passages.t: Not like Egypt, not like Canaan
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses to say to Israel, ‘I am the LORD your God’ (verse 2).

“You must not follow the practices of the land of Egypt, where you used to live, and you must not follow the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you. You must not walk in their customs” (verse 3).

“You are to practice My judgments and keep My statutes by walking in them. I am the LORD your God” (verse 4). “Keep My statutes and My judgments, for the man who does these things will live by them. I am the LORD” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The book now turns from the altar to the household. Israel stands between two worlds, Egypt behind and Canaan ahead. It has been rescued from one and promised the other, and it is told to take its way of life from neither.

The chapter is framed, at its start and its end, by the words ‘I am the LORD your God’. They are the words that open the Ten Commandments. The laws between are not presented as custom or taste. They rest on who God is and on what he has done for this people.

Verse 5 gives the purpose. God's statutes are given as a way of life: the person who does them ‘will live by them’. The law describes how a rescued people can flourish. It is not set out as a list of things spoiled for the sake of spoiling them.

Chapter 20 will come back to many of the acts named in this chapter and attach penalties. This chapter states the principles.
passages.later:
Ezekiel repeats verse 5 when he retells Israel's story: God gave them his statutes, “for the man who does these things will live by them” (Ezekiel 20:11).

Paul quotes the verse twice, to describe the righteousness that is by the law: “The man who does these things will live by them” (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12). He sets beside it the righteousness that comes by faith. On the common reading, his point is not that the law was bad but that no one has kept it fully.
passages.asks: Israel was told not to copy the place it came from or the place it was going. Ask which of your own habits you have simply taken from the world you grew up in, or from the one you want to belong to. And ask whether you think of God's commands as a fence or as a way to live.

passages.happening:
“None of you are to approach any close relative to have sexual relations. I am the LORD” (verse 6).

A list follows. A man must not have sexual relations with his mother, his father's wife, his sister or half-sister, his granddaughter, his aunt, his daughter-in-law or his brother's wife (verses 7-16). He must not take both a woman and her daughter or granddaughter (verse 17), or marry his wife's sister as a rival to her while she lives (verse 18).

Reasons are given along the way: “She is your mother” (verse 7); “that would shame your family” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Households in ancient Israel were large and close. Several generations of one family, with wives who had married in from other clans, might live in a single compound. These laws protected the people in that house. Sisters, half-sisters, stepdaughters and daughters-in-law could live near the men of the family and be safe from them.

That is the heart of the passage. The family is to be a safe place. The lines are drawn round the people with least power to protect themselves.

The Hebrew behind ‘have sexual relations’ is a frank old phrase, to uncover someone's nakedness. The word for nakedness comes twenty-four times in the chapter. It carries a sense of shame and exposure. The laws picture this kind of wrong as exposing and dishonoring a person.

The laws are spoken mainly to men. In that world they were the heads of households and held the power in the home. The law puts the duty where the power was.

Some of these unions had happened in Israel's own past. Abraham married his half-sister, and Jacob married two sisters. The chapter does not comment on them. It marks a break. What was once done is now forbidden to God's people.
passages.later:
These laws were still alive centuries later. John the Baptist told Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18), and it cost him his life.

Paul was appalled to hear of a man in the church at Corinth who ‘has his father’s wife’ (1 Corinthians 5:1).
passages.hard:
What does this passage say to someone who was harmed inside a family?

It says that God's law is on your side. The first thing this chapter does, before anything else, is to forbid a man to use the women and girls of his own household. What it forbids, it forbids to the one with power. It lays no blame on the one who was used.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law made the home a place where the weaker members were to be safe from the stronger. Ask whether everyone in your home is safe, and feels safe. And ask what your church does to protect children and others who could be harmed by someone they trust.

passages.happening:
A man must not approach a woman for sexual relations during her period (verse 19). “You must not lie carnally with your neighbor’s wife and thus defile yourself with her” (verse 20).

“You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech, for you must not profane the name of your God. I am the LORD” (verse 21).

“You must not lie with a man as with a woman; that is an abomination” (verse 22).

No one, man or woman, is to have sexual relations with an animal (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The list now moves outside the family.

Verse 20 repeats the commandment against adultery.

Verse 21 stands out, because it is not about sex. It forbids giving a child to Molech. Elsewhere in the Old Testament the name is linked with the Ammonites, and with a place outside Jerusalem called Topheth, in the Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned. Scholars debate whether Molech was the name of a god or of a kind of sacrifice. Either way, what is condemned is the ritual killing of children. Leviticus forbids it without exception. It comes in this list because it, too, is a use of the family's own flesh that God will not have.

Verse 22 is taken up in the hard question below.

The word ‘abomination’ in verse 22 translates the Hebrew to'evah, something detestable. In verses 26 to 30 the same word is used of the whole list of practices in this chapter. Elsewhere in the Bible it is used of idolatry, of dishonest scales and of pride. It is not a special word for sexual sin.
passages.later:
Jeremiah speaks of the place where children were burned, and gives God's own word on it: it was “something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). King Josiah later destroyed the place, “so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech” (2 Kings 23:10).

Paul's Jewish hearers knew this law. In his letter to the Romans, the sins he lists also include envy, slander and disobedience to parents, and his next sentence turns on the reader: “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another” (Romans 2:1).
passages.hard:
What does verse 22 say, and how do Christians read it?

The verse says, “You must not lie with a man as with a woman; that is an abomination.” Like most of the chapter it is spoken to the men of Israel, and it forbids sexual relations between men. These notes state that plainly and do not soften it.

Christians read the verse in more than one way. The historic reading of the church, and still the reading of most churches today, is that it speaks of same-sex sexual acts as such. On this reading the wording names no particular setting, such as a temple or an exploitative relationship. The verse stands among laws Christians still hold, against incest, adultery and the sacrifice of children. It rests on God's creation of humanity as male and female (Genesis 1:27). And the New Testament takes up the Old Testament's teaching on sex while it sets aside the food and purity laws. Some Christians read it differently. They hold that the verse addressed particular practices of the ancient world, which they see as tied to the worship of other gods or marked by exploitation, so that it did not have in view faithful, committed same-sex relationships. Some add that Christians already set aside other laws in these chapters, such as the ban on cloth woven of two materials (19:19). Those who hold the historic reading answer that the wording of the law is general, and that the New Testament itself repeats the sexual laws while it releases the others. These notes set out both readings. Faithful Christians disagree here, and these notes take no side.

Three things are plain on any reading. First, this law stands beside laws against adultery, slander, hatred in the heart and dishonest dealing (verse 20; 19:11-18), so that no reader stands outside it. Second, the New Testament speaks grace to people with every kind of past: “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Third, nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

And one thing more must be said plainly. No one may use this verse to harm or shame any person. Anyone who uses it as a reason to mock, to threaten, to shut out of a home or to strike is misusing it. The same book commands, ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ (19:18).

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law that forbade these acts also forbade the killing of children for a god. Ask what your own world gives its children up to: ambition, money, neglect, a parent's anger. And ask whether you have ever used a verse of the Bible to look down on another person, and what it would mean to turn the same book's light on yourself first.

passages.happening:
“Do not defile yourselves by any of these practices, for by all these things the nations I am driving out before you have defiled themselves” (verse 24). “Even the land has become defiled, so I am punishing it for its sin, and the land will vomit out its inhabitants” (verse 25).

Israel and the foreigner living in Israel alike are to keep God's statutes (verse 26). “So if you defile the land, it will vomit you out as it spewed out the nations before you” (verse 28).

The chapter closes as it opened: “I am the LORD your God” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The picture is startling and bodily. The land is like a body that cannot keep down what poisons it. In Leviticus the land is not just property. It is God's, and it answers to how people live on it.

This is the second kind of defilement the book knows. Chapters 11 to 15 spoke of a ritual uncleanness that was not sin and that washing took away. Here grave wrongs are said to defile people, and the land with them. No washing removes that.

Notice who is warned. The nations before Israel are not condemned for who they were. They are condemned for what was done. And Israel is told, in the same breath, that it will be treated in exactly the same way if it does the same things. There is one standard. The warning in this chapter is aimed at Israel.

That is how Israel's own writers later read their history. When the people were carried into exile, the prophets explained it with this chapter's words.

These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern. The peoples named here are not a name for anyone living today, and this passage gives no one permission to hate or harm any people or to claim any land.
passages.later:
Long before, God had told Abraham that he would wait: “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16).

After the exile, Ezra prayed in the words of this chapter. The land, he said, was ‘polluted by the impurity of its peoples’ (Ezra 9:11), and his prayer is a confession of Israel's own guilt.

A psalm grieves over Israel's own child sacrifice, and says what it did: “the land was polluted with blood” (Psalm 106:38).
passages.asks: Israel was warned that it would be judged by the standard it saw applied to others. Ask where you condemn in another people, party or church what you excuse in your own. And ask what your way of life is doing to the place where you live, and to those who will live there after you.
